read: partial: main text pp.1-9 in full (abstract, introduction, related work, section 3 benchmark creation and MARJ, section 4 experiments, section 5 analysis incl. 5.2 reliability of evaluation, 5.3 error analysis, 5.4 data leakage, conclusion); appendix A-B (pp.14-17) and Tables 13-14 (pp.19-20) read; result tables, prompts, case studies (pp.18, 21-29) and references skimmed
venue_now: ICML 2025, PMLR 267 (page 1 footer); the file is arXiv:2502.00334v4, 3 Jun 2025 (p.1). The May reference list prints it as an arXiv preprint.
what_it_is: An undergraduate physics problem-solving benchmark of 5,520 problems, each in Chinese and English (11,040 in all), covering 3 domains, 13 subjects and 59 topics, with seven answer types (pp.1-2, 4). The problems come from seven exercise books ('The Great Compendium of Physics Problems', USTC), OCR'd with Mathpix, manually corrected, deduplicated, with image problems, proofs, estimations and explanations removed and multi-part problems split (p.4). Answers are scored by MARJ: type-specific rule matching first (numbers within 1e-2 relative error), then GPT-4o re-judges the answers the rules mark wrong (p.5, pp.16-17). 31 LLMs are evaluated; the best, o1-mini, reaches 49.8% (p.1, p.6).
domain: undergraduate physics: mechanics and thermodynamics, electromagnetism (incl. optics), modern physics; 13 subjects incl. solid-state and semiconductor physics, topics incl. fluid mechanics and circuit analysis (pp.19-20)
size: 5,520 problems x 2 languages = 11,040 items; 13 subjects, 59 topics; 31 LLMs in the main evaluation (p.1, p.5), plus Phi-4 and DeepSeek-R1 added in Table 5 (p.7)
source_of_items: textbooks (seven undergraduate physics exercise books, originally in Chinese and translated into English; p.4)
has_gold_traces: partial: each item keeps the source book's worked solution in a Problem-Solution-Answer format (p.4; average 318.5 solution tokens, Table 2 p.4), but solutions play no part in scoring, which checks only final answers (p.5)
evaluation: final answer: MARJ, rule-based matching per answer type (numerical answers compared on the scientific-notation base with up to 1e-2 relative error; expressions normalised by removing physical constants) followed by a GPT-4o judge for answers the rules reject (p.5, pp.16-17)
human_validation: The team manually reviewed and corrected the OCR'd PDFs and LaTeX files (p.4). MARJ agreed with the authors' own annotation on 98% of a random 100 examples (p.7); who annotated and any agreement statistic are not reported. Human evaluators labelled 100 incorrect o1-mini answers by error type (p.8). The reasoning-skill labels are assigned by GPT-4o, not by humans (p.4).
contamination_measures: n-gram leakage detection (5-gram accuracy, following Xu et al. 2024a) on eight models: 0.0% to 0.75% of items flagged as contaminated (pp.8-9, Table 6); embedding-based deduplication (p.4). Items are static and come from published exercise books.

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180, uncited, covers all six): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: The gist is right: UGPhysics tests undergraduate physics problem solving, and 'Laws Application' is one of its four labelled skills (p.4; definitions p.14). But the label fits only part of it: in Table 14 (p.20) Math Derivation is the largest skill (4,440 of 11,040 items), ahead of Laws Application (3,914), Knowledge Recall (1,168) and Practical Application (1,106), and the skill labels are GPT-4o's (p.4). 'Effectively' is an endorsement the paper's evidence does not address. S-P2's 'theoretical physics' is loose: UGPhysics is undergraduate textbook physics, including fluid mechanics, circuit analysis and semiconductor transport (pp.19-20), not theoretical physics as a field; 'lacking the integrative context of engineering' is a fair contrast. The May text does not state what matters most for EngTrace's comparison, that UGPhysics is static textbook material scored on final answers only (pp.4-5), though the closing 'outcome matching' sentence (L199-201) is accurate for it.

suggested_wording: UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) collects 5,520 undergraduate physics exercises from textbook problem books and scores only the final answer, with rule-based matching backed by an LLM judge.
facts_to_cite: 5,520 undergraduate-level physics problems, each in English and Chinese (11,040 items), 13 subjects, 59 topics, seven answer types (p.1, p.2, Table 2 p.4)
Sourced from seven undergraduate physics exercise books (The Great Compendium of Physics Problems, USTC), OCR'd and manually corrected (p.4)
Scoring is final-answer only: rule-based matching first, then GPT-4o re-judges the answers the rules mark wrong (MARJ, p.5); numerical answers allow up to 1e-2 relative error (p.5)
MARJ agreed with human annotation on 98% of 100 randomly selected examples (p.7)
31 LLMs evaluated; best overall accuracy 49.8% (o1-mini) (p.1, p.6)
Math-specialised LLMs gain little over their general-purpose counterparts on UGPhysics (Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct +0.14 points, 72B +3.3 points) (p.6)
Data leakage checked by 5-gram accuracy on eight models; 0.0% to 0.75% of items flagged (pp.8-9)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: quantitative, multi-step problems in topics adjacent to EngTrace's (thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, circuit analysis, semiconductor physics; pp.19-20); answer checking with a relative tolerance; a rule-first cascade that sends only rule-rejected answers to an LLM judge, which parallels EngTrace's deterministic checks with a residual judge (p.5). Lacks: generated instances (static book problems); use of gold traces in scoring (solutions exist but only final answers are judged); any step-level or process evaluation; an engineering domain; validation of the evaluator beyond a 100-item check against the authors' annotation with no agreement statistic (p.7). It has bilingual items, which EngTrace does not.
notes: Reference-list error (confirmed on p.1): the May entry prints 'Xingyu Xu, Qian Xu, Tong Xiao, Tao Chen, Yufan Yan, Jifan Zhang, Shuo Diao, Chen Yang, and Yizhong Wang'; the authors are Xin Xu, Qiyun Xu, Tong Xiao, Tianhao Chen, Yuchen Yan, Jiaxin Zhang, Shizhe Diao, Can Yang, Yang Wang. Update the entry to ICML 2025 (PMLR 267). The finding that math-specialised models gain little on physics (p.6) echoes the May paper's math-pretraining claim, which the state brief says is dropped; do not use UGPhysics to revive it. Table 2 lists 'Total Difficulty Level 4' (p.4) without defining difficulty anywhere I read.
